newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Uncertainties halt Taiwan stock bull run - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Uncertainties halt Taiwan stock bull run - analysts.

text.p: Taiwan stocks tumbled on Friday as investors dumped shares they saw as overvalued, and analysts said they expected further declines amid political and economic uncertainties.

The weighted index fell 298.66 points, or 3.52 percent, to finish at 8,187.00, marking the heaviest single-day loss in 15 months. Turnover was an active T$121.6 billion, but much lighter than the hectic volumes during the market's recent bull run.

Despite a newspaper report that the combined net profit of the 386 listed firms had surged a year-on-year 43 percent to T$70.62 billion in the first quarter, brokers said many firms' equity prices had outperformed their fundamentals.
"Many investors are disappointed after realising their companies' share prices did not match the performances," said Albert Lin, an analyst at Golden Securities.
National Securities analyst Alex Yang said: "The companies' first-quarter profits are not bad at all, but people's expectations were too high."

Taiwan's stock market had been one of the world's hottest in 1997. The index had risen 27 percent this year before a downward correction set in on Monday. It has fallen nearly 500 points, or 5.4 percent, since Monday.
Concerns over the island's social, political and economic outlooks were likely to prolong the correction, analysts said.

The central bank recently continued to issue negotiable certificates of deposit to mop up banking system liquidity. The bank has confirmed it was responding to the liquidity situation but denied that it was motivated by the recent stock rally.
Investors were worried that the central bank may further tighten its monetary policy during the May 8 board meeting, analysts said.

"It's clear the government wants to lower the stock market's temperature at the moment, and many people are driven to the sidelines because of the government's attitude," said Lin Long-hsien of United Securities.
Amy Huang, analyst for Nomura Securities, said caution was intensified by the National Assembly's planned meeting on political reforms and concerns over deteriorating law and order.
The murder of a Taiwan actress's daughter in a US$5 million ransom case has caused a public outcry and many said business confidence would be dampened if the crime situation worsened.
"There is a general lack of confidence because of all these uncertainties," Huang said. "It's not a good time to chase higher share prices."
Brokers did not rule out the possibility that the index may fall below the key 8,000-point support level in the near term.
"There is little doubt that the market will continue to consolidate. It's difficult to say how long the consolidation will last," Huang said.
